texto:
Netflix on October 20, 2026 lowered its expectation for 2026 advertising revenue to about $2.7 billion from roughly $3 billion, blaming a slower rollout of ad products and partner integrations, while reporting third-quarter revenue of $12.87 billion, up 11.8% year over year, and an operating margin of 34.6%. Full-year revenue guidance landed at $51.1 billion, 0.2% below the midpoint of the previous range, because subscription revenue made up most of the shortfall.
In Short
Netflix said it will earn about $2.7 billion from ads this year instead of the $3 billion it promised, because some of the advertising tools it is building with partners arrived late. Its ad business is still growing more than 80% this year, and the company as a whole made more money than a year ago, so the miss is small next to its $51.1 billion in yearly sales. If you buy or sell TV advertising, the practical change is that some Netflix ad products are behind schedule, while the ad plan itself is still heading to 12 more countries in March 2027.
The quarter in numbers
Netflix published its third-quarter shareholder letter on October 20, 2026, followed the same afternoon by a video earnings interview at 1:45pm Pacific time with co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos, chief financial officer Spence Neumann and Spencer Wang, VP of Finance and Capital Markets. The quarter ran to September 30.
Revenue for the three months reached $12,874 million, according to the consolidated statements, compared with $11,510 million a year earlier. The exact growth rate in the company's own summary table is 11.8%; the letter rounds that to 12%, and to 11% on a foreign exchange neutral basis. Operating income rose 37% to $4,459 million. Net income was $3,664 million against $2,547 million in the third quarter of 2025, and diluted earnings per share came to $0.87 versus $0.59, a 49% increase on the unrounded figures.
How did that compare with outside expectations? The transcript of the call, published by S&P Global Market Intelligence and labeled a preliminary copy, lists a consensus revenue estimate of $12,874.33 million, almost exactly the $12,874.18 million Netflix reported. Earnings per share beat the $0.82 consensus. At the second-quarter report in July, Netflix had guided to 11.7% growth for the third quarter, according to PPC Land's coverage of the Q2 results, which put implied revenue at $12.86 billion. The outcome came in slightly above that.
The margin story is where the quarter departed from forecast. According to the letter, operating income and margin "were ahead of forecast due primarily to the timing of expenses and the slight upside in revenue." The 34.6% margin compares with 28.2% a year earlier and 33.4% in the second quarter of 2026.
The workbook Netflix posted alongside the letter shows where the expense lines moved. Cost of revenues fell to $6,079 million from $6,164 million a year earlier, a decline of about 1.4% by PPC Land's calculation, while content amortization rose to $4,235 million from $4,003 million. Technology and development grew fastest, up roughly 21% to $1,033 million. Sales and marketing rose about 6.5% to $837 million, and general and administrative expenses rose about 2% to $466 million. Stock-based compensation climbed to $134 million from $81 million.
The provision for income taxes was $653 million on pre-tax income of $4,317 million, an effective rate of about 15.1% by PPC Land's calculation.
Regional revenue
All four regions grew, though each decelerated on a foreign exchange neutral basis compared with the second quarter:
- UCAN (United States and Canada): $5,628 million, up 11% reported and 11% F/X neutral.
- EMEA: $4,107 million, up 11% reported and 9% F/X neutral.
- LATAM: $1,603 million, up 17% reported and 12% F/X neutral.
- APAC: $1,537 million, up 12% reported and 15% F/X neutral.
EMEA's 9% F/X neutral rate was its lowest in the five quarters shown in the letter, down from 15% in the third quarter of 2025. LATAM fell from 20% to 12% over the same period.
The Q3 letter contains no membership total. It describes the audience instead as "approaching one billion people," a figure that counts people rather than accounts. The most recent count PPC Land reported was more than 325 million paid memberships at the end of 2025, disclosed with the Q4 2025 results.
The ad revenue reset
For PPC Land readers, the central number in the letter is a single line in the guidance section. "We currently expect 2026 ad revenue of ~$2.7B vs. approximately $3B previously," the letter states, "due to slightly slower than expected rollout of some ad product capabilities."
That $3 billion target has followed Netflix all year. Peters set it in January, when the company reported that 2025 ad revenue had surpassed $1.5 billion and said it expected advertising to roughly double in 2026, as PPC Land reported on January 21. It was repeated with the Q1 2026 results in April, at the May 13 upfront, and again in July, when Netflix said advertising was on track for about $3 billion.
The new figure is about 10% lower. In absolute terms, roughly $300 million of expected ad revenue has gone. Yet the full-year revenue forecast moved far less. Netflix narrowed its 2026 range to $51.0 billion to $51.4 billion in July; the new $51.1 billion forecast is $100 million below that $51.2 billion midpoint. The letter explains the gap: "subscription revenue growth has outperformed our expectations." Put plainly, subscribers covered about two thirds of the ad shortfall.
On the call, Peters framed the miss as the cost of an aggressive plan rather than a demand problem.
"We set big growth targets for our ads business this year. We established an aggressive product road map that was consistent with that strategy," he said. "But we are currently a bit behind our aggressive target for the year. We're still growing, our ads business over 80% this year."
Growth of just over 80% on a 2025 base of a little over $1.5 billion is consistent with the $2.7 billion figure, by PPC Land's calculation. At $2.7 billion, advertising would account for about 5.3% of Netflix's forecast 2026 revenue.
What slipped
Peters was specific about the cause, even if he did not name products. "We've seen some delays in the rollout and partner integrations for some of those new ads products," he said. "So getting to the integration model that we want sometimes takes a bit more work with our partners, but we strongly believe that a modest short-term hit for a better long-term strategic position is a good ultimate trade-off."
The integration model he described is one in which partners' data and tools connect to Netflix without the company giving up its own data. Netflix wants to bring "the best of digital advertising to the best of TV advertising, all while respecting our member privacy and ensuring that we also retain our first-party data advantage," Peters said. "So our integration models, our partner integration models preserve that advantage while getting to the best targeting that we can."
He also made a claim that is difficult to verify independently: "I think that the build-out that we've been on is the fastest build-out of a comparable ad stack in our industry." No benchmark was offered.
Which partner integrations were late? Neither the letter nor the call says. PPC Land's earlier reporting gives the list of integrations Netflix had committed to this year. In March, Netflix added Amazon DSP audience targeting, Yahoo DSP deterministic signals and its own Conversion API, and Amazon Audiences reached Netflix inventory in EMEA on May 18. At the upfront, Netflix said Amazon DSP audience targeting would extend to all ad-supported countries by June 1, 2026, with Yahoo DSP following in the months after. It also promised clean room partners Snowflake and AWS, with InfoSum due by the end of 2026, and said Pause Ads and live content would become programmatically buyable in the US and Canada in the summer, with other countries by year end. The Q3 materials do not say which of these dates moved.
Peters insisted the demand side was not the problem. Asked by Vikram Kesavabhotla of Baird about demand and the breadth of advertisers, he said "general demand remains strong, breadth of advertisers continues to expand, and ultimately, advertisers want our new products and features, and that's a big mechanism of growth for us." No updated advertiser count was given; the most recent figure, from April, was more than 4,000 active advertisers, up 70% year over year.
Ad tech changes in the quarter
The letter lists the third-quarter changes to the Netflix Ads Suite, the company's in-house ad technology stack:
- Programmatic access extended "through globally-available CTV marketplace deals."
- New partnerships with MercadoLibre in LATAM and AdForm in EMEA. The letter spells the Danish company "AdForm"; the company itself uses Adform.
- Measurement capabilities expanding "to in-DSP measurement including reach, frequency, and attribution."
The Adform reference is the more consequential of the two partnerships for European buyers. Adform runs its own DSP, ad server and SSP from Copenhagen. In the PDF, the words "in EMEA" link to a Netflix news post titled "Netflix hosts first UK upfront," which suggests the partnership was disclosed at that event. MercadoLibre, the Latin American e-commerce company, brings a retail data set to the LATAM inventory, though the letter gives no detail on how the partnership works.
The marketplace change continues a shift that began in July, when Netflix joined The Trade Desk's Sellers and Publishers 500+ marketplace, removing spend minimums for buyers who had previously reached Netflix only through programmatic guaranteed or private marketplace deals. Netflix's programmatic partners now include The Trade Desk, Google Display & Video 360, Magnite, Microsoft, Yahoo DSP and Amazon DSP. In-DSP measurement of reach, frequency and attribution matters for buyers who plan and report inside a demand-side platform rather than relying on Netflix's own reports.
The gap between ad and ad-free plans
Robert Fishman of MoffettNathanson asked about the difference in average revenue per membership, or ARM, between the ad-supported tier and the standard plan without ads. Peters said the ad plan still earns less, though the difference is shrinking. He did not give numbers.
"We managed the ads business for total revenue and growth. So we look at ARM and fill rates as means to an end, not an end goal in and of itself," he said. The gap, he added, "means underrealized revenue growth for us in the near term."
His explanation of how that gap closes is a description of two simultaneous effects. More demand sources, more ad products, more measurement and easier transacting raise fill rates and push ad-tier ARM higher. At the same time, more members on the ad plan increase the inventory available. Peters said he expected "this dual growth phenomenon where we're growing inventory and growing into our monetization of that inventory" to persist "for some time."
For buyers, that combination usually means supply growing faster than prices can firm. The US ad plan costs $8.99 a month, a price PPC Land reported with the Q1 results.
Ad plan heads to 12 countries in March 2027
The letter repeats that Netflix "will introduce our advertising tier to 15 new countries in 2027," and adds a date for the first group. "The first tranche of new market launches will happen in March 2027: nine countries in EMEA, Colombia, Peru and New Zealand (a new addition from our previous announcement)."
That is 12 of the 15. At the May upfront, Netflix named all 15: Austria, Belgium, Colombia, Denmark, Indonesia, Ireland, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Peru, the Philippines, Poland, Sweden, Switzerland and Thailand. Nine of those are in EMEA, matching the letter's count. By elimination, the three countries not in the March tranche would be Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand - a PPC Land inference, since the letter does not name them.
The "new addition" language needs care. New Zealand was already on the list of 15 presented in May, so the phrase appears to refer to New Zealand joining the March group, rather than to a 16th country. PPC Land had separately reported that the ad plan would reach nine EMEA countries on March 1, 2027; that article could not be retrieved during research for this piece, so the precise day in March is not confirmed here.
On the call, Peters described the expansion as "our first expansion of ads countries since we launched."
His answer to Sean Diffley of Morgan Stanley set out where advertising fits in Netflix's country-by-country model. In the most penetrated markets, he named the US, UK and Australia, "our revenue growth drivers in those markets are going to skew towards ARM and advertising growth." In newer markets such as Indonesia and Colombia, member growth matters most. Mexico and Japan sit in the middle, as ad markets where both members and ARM can grow. The Philippines and Turkey were cited as countries that do not yet have an ad plan.
Guidance for Q4 and the full year
Netflix forecasts fourth-quarter revenue of $13,442 million, which the summary table puts at 11.5% growth and the letter rounds to 12%, or 11% F/X neutral. Operating income is forecast at $3,500 million for a 26.0% margin, compared with 24.5% a year earlier. Diluted EPS is forecast at $0.67.
That Q4 revenue forecast sits below the $13,525.16 million consensus listed in the S&P Global transcript, and the EPS forecast is below the $0.73 consensus. The consensus table in the transcript appears misaligned: it shows $51,100 million, Netflix's 2026 revenue guidance, in a column labeled as fiscal 2027 consensus.
For the full year, the letter's figures are:
- Revenue of $51.1 billion, up 13% (12% F/X neutral).
- Operating margin of 31.5% (31.4% at January 1, 2026 exchange rates), against 29.5% in 2025.
- Operating income growth of more than 20%.
- Free cash flow of about $12.0 billion, down from a prior projection of $12.5 billion.
PPC Land checked the arithmetic. Nine-month revenue of $37,684 million plus the $13,442 million fourth-quarter forecast gives $51,126 million. Nine-month operating income of $12,608 million plus $3,500 million gives $16,108 million, a 31.5% margin and growth of about 21% on 2025's $13,327 million. The figures in the letter, the transcript and the workbook agree on every reported statement line PPC Land compared.
Headcount reductions
The fourth-quarter margin includes "~120 basis points negative impact associated with our recently announced headcount reductions," according to the letter. For the full year, the impact is about 30 basis points. On the fourth-quarter revenue forecast, 120 basis points equals roughly $160 million, by PPC Land's calculation. The letter does not state the number of roles affected. Dan Kurnos of StoneX described the reductions on the call as the largest since 2022.
Peters explained the reasoning without giving numbers. "When you've driven considerable top line growth as we have over the last several years and you're in a highly dynamic market that's constantly changing, I don't think it's unusual then to find that there are some areas that we built quickly and we ended up over invested in," he said. Netflix prefers to make such changes gradually, he added, "but sometimes, the team needs a forcing function."
Neumann declined to quantify annual savings or how much would flow to 2027 margins. "We're not going to specifically quantify the expense impact in 2027," he said, adding that 2027 guidance, including margin, will come in January.
2027
Neumann said "it's premature to issue full year 2027 guidance" but that the targets were unchanged. "We look to sustain double-digit revenue growth. We look to expand margins, and we look to increase free cash flow," he said, naming member growth, pricing and ads as the three revenue levers.
Engagement and view hours
Netflix acknowledged the question hanging over the stock. "We know there's some investor concern about our view hours growth," the letter states. It argues that the reaction to 2026 price increases, which it describes as "consistent with prior price changes and our expectations," shows engagement is healthy.
Churn is the company's main evidence. Globally and in the US, churn improved year over year in the third quarter and was better than forecast, according to the letter. Peters added an external comparison: "Netflix subscribers are paying the least per hour of viewing compared to other SVOD offerings in the country," referring to the US, and in some cases rivals cost "more than double per hour."
Neumann was blunter. "And to be clear, we want to grow view hours faster. We're not satisfied. We're working on it," he said.
The concern is not new. In August, a Simulmedia analysis found that 89% of 73 comparable returning Netflix series drew fewer views than their previous season, and that total viewing grew 4.5% between the first half of 2023 and the first half of 2026. For advertisers, slower viewing growth limits how quickly ad inventory can expand from engagement alone, which puts more weight on new members and new markets.
India as the counterexample
The letter offers India as proof that the model works when the slate does. Lock Upp, Netflix's first daily reality series, drove "the most viewing of any title on Netflix in India ever," based on view hours in the first 91 days. View hours in India grew 24% year over year, and view hours per member grew low-to-mid single digits. Combined with a transaction-based loyalty bundle with Flipkart, Netflix had its largest quarter of paid net additions in India.
Here the sources disagree. The letter says Q3 revenue in India grew "~18% year over year on a F/X neutral basis." On the call, both Peters and Neumann described the figure as "nearly 20%." The letter's number is the written disclosure; the executives' rounding is generous.
The US slate and a new content chief
Sarandos was direct about the US. "It's just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we'd like," he said. "There is no need for a fundamental shift in the strategy. We do need better execution in the U.S."
That execution is now the responsibility of Peter Rice, who joins as Chief Content Officer. Sarandos thanked Bela Bajaria, whose "decade long run" he credited with building the international team. He said Rice, who has run TV networks, film studios and streaming services, "understands talent relations."
The company's third-quarter hits were largely non-English. The letter says non-English viewing has grown from under 10% of total viewing a decade ago to more than a third now. The Last House was the largest title listed, with 91 million views. Netflix defines a view as hours viewed divided by runtime, measured over the first 91 days.
Licensing, live and TF1
Netflix spent much of the call explaining how third-party content fits a strategy built on originals. Sarandos said "roughly 95% of our spend and nearly all of our revenue is focused on that core" of series, films and live events.
Licensing deals mentioned include Disney, which brought all five Ice Age films to the service ahead of Disney's February 2027 theatrical release of Ice Age: Boiling Point, and a Globo agreement in Brazil that Sarandos called "the most meaningful licensing deal we've ever done in Brazil." He also noted the complication: "all of our suppliers are also our competitors."
The TF1 integration in France is the most relevant third-party arrangement for advertisers. TF1's channels went live inside Netflix in France on June 19, 2026, with TF1 keeping control of its own advertising inventory. An image in the shareholder letter shows the TF1+ row on the Netflix TV interface with the French label "Comprend des pubs," meaning the content includes ads. Peters said "the early analysis and testing that we've done indicates that the TF1 engagement is incremental to our platform," and that TF1 viewing on Netflix is growing every month.
Asked about add-on subscription services, including hybrid ad and subscription services, Peters said "there's nothing to announce today," while describing such services as "yet another way to expand our entertainment offering." For broadcasters weighing similar deals, the TF1 model, where the partner keeps its ad sales, is the reference case.
Live events remain an ad story. Sarandos said they "add fuel to our ad revenues." The fourth quarter includes Netflix's biggest live slate to date: the NFL's first Thanksgiving Eve game, a Christmas Day doubleheader and the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua fight. Those are the inventory that brand advertisers buy through upfront commitments, and their timing in Q4 will shape whether the reduced $2.7 billion figure holds.
On theatrical releases, Sarandos said Netflix would release about 30 films in cinemas this year, and that the company has begun reporting box office grosses. He said La Bola Negra opened with a per-screen average of more than $69,000. The preliminary transcript spells the title differently; the letter's spelling is used here.
Cash, buybacks and debt
Net cash from operating activities was $3,162 million in the quarter, and free cash flow was $2,884 million, against $2,660 million a year earlier. The lower full-year free cash flow forecast of about $12.0 billion is due "primarily to the expected closing of a real estate transaction in Q4," according to the letter. Nine-month free cash flow stands at $9,503 million, which implies roughly $2.5 billion in the fourth quarter, by PPC Land's calculation.
The nine-month figure is inflated by a one-off. The workbook shows $2,852 million of "interest and other income" in the first quarter, which PPC Land's Q1 report attributed to the termination fee from the abandoned Warner Bros. transaction. That explains why nine-month net income of $12,348 million is so far ahead of 2025's $8,563 million.
Netflix bought back 63.9 million shares for $4.8 billion in the quarter, which the letter calls "our largest quarter ever of stock repurchases." That implies an average price of about $75 a share, by PPC Land's calculation. Repurchases totaled $10.8 billion in the first nine months, and $22.3 billion of authorization remains.
The letter puts gross debt at $15.3 billion and cash and cash equivalents at $8.2 billion. The balance sheet shows short-term and long-term debt totaling $15,132 million; the difference is debt issuance costs and a fair value hedging adjustment, listed in the net debt reconciliation, which arrives at net debt of $7,114 million. The letter says gross debt rose about $1 billion from the second quarter after a $1 billion bond deal to fund a $1 billion maturity in the fourth quarter. On the carrying values in the balance sheet, the increase is about $823 million.
Content spending ran ahead of amortization. Additions to content assets were $5,160 million in the quarter, against amortization of $4,235 million. Over nine months the ratio is about 1.17 times by PPC Land's calculation, slightly above the "~1.1x" the company expects for the full year.
Why this matters for advertisers
Netflix is still small in advertising relative to its subscription business, at about 5% of revenue. But it has become one of the more closely watched premium AVOD suppliers because of the speed of its build-out and its decision to open inventory to every major DSP.
The revised figure tells buyers three things. First, the company's targets for new ad products and partner integrations were too ambitious for 2026, and some capabilities promised at the upfront are later than planned. Second, Netflix is choosing to protect its first-party data position over speed when partner integrations require compromises. Third, demand, by the company's account, was not the cause.
What the materials do not say is which products slipped, how large the ARM gap between plans is, or how many advertisers are now active. Those questions will likely return in January, when Netflix gives 2027 guidance, which should include its first ad revenue target for the year in which the ad plan enters 12 new countries.

- March 2026 - Netflix adds Amazon DSP audience targeting, Yahoo DSP signals and its own Conversion API.
- April 16, 2026 - Q1 2026 results: revenue of $12.25 billion, $2.8 billion Warner Bros. termination fee booked in other income, ads target held at about $3 billion.

- May 18, 2026 - Amazon Audiences reach Netflix inventory in EMEA.
- June 19, 2026 - TF1 channels go live inside Netflix in France.
- July 16, 2026 - Q2 2026 results: revenue guidance narrowed to $51.0 billion to $51.4 billion, ads still tracking to about $3 billion.
- July 20, 2026 - Netflix joins The Trade Desk's Sellers and Publishers 500+ marketplace without spend minimums.
- August 6, 2026 - Simulmedia analysis finds 89% of returning Netflix series lost viewers.
- Q3 2026 - Netflix extends programmatic access through global CTV marketplace deals and adds MercadoLibre in LATAM and Adform in EMEA.
- September 30, 2026 - Third quarter ends.
- October 18, 2026 - Cut-off date for view counts in the Q3 letter.
- October 20, 2026 - Netflix publishes Q3 results, lowers 2026 ad revenue expectation to about $2.7 billion, and holds its earnings interview at 1:45pm PT.
- Q4 2026 - Headcount reductions weigh about 120 basis points on the quarter's margin; NFL Thanksgiving Eve and Christmas Day games; expected real estate transaction closes.
- February 2027 - Disney's theatrical release of Ice Age: Boiling Point.
- March 2027 - Ad plan arrives in nine EMEA countries, Colombia, Peru and New Zealand.

Summary
Who: Netflix, its co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos, CFO Spence Neumann and VP of Finance and Capital Markets Spencer Wang, along with advertising partners including MercadoLibre and Adform.
What: Netflix reported Q3 2026 revenue of $12.87 billion, up 11.8%, with a 34.6% operating margin, and lowered its 2026 ad revenue expectation to about $2.7 billion from roughly $3 billion because of slower rollout of ad products and partner integrations. It forecast 2026 revenue of $51.1 billion and confirmed the ad plan will launch in nine EMEA countries, Colombia, Peru and New Zealand in March 2027.
When: The shareholder letter and earnings interview were published on October 20, 2026, covering the quarter that ended September 30, 2026.
Where: Results cover Netflix's global business across UCAN, EMEA, LATAM and APAC, with the 2027 ad plan expansion focused on EMEA, Latin America and New Zealand.
Why: The ad target cut matters to advertisers and agencies because it shows that ad products and partner integrations promised for 2026 are running late, even as Netflix says demand is strong and the ad business is growing more than 80% this year.
